..

I.

Introduction

[
1
]

The claimant applied to enforce the terms of a separation
agreement; the respondent cross-applied under
s. 44(4)
of the
Family Law
Act,
S.B.C. 2011, c. 25 [
FLA
],
to vary
the agreement. The separation agreement and portions of the respondent’s notice
of application were ordered to stand as pleadings and the matter was referred
for trial.

[
2
]

The claimant seeks to enforce a term providing
for the parties’ children to attend school on the North Shore as of September
2022. The respondent seeks to vary that term to provide for the children to attend
school in Gibsons.

[
3
]

A bottom-line decision was provided on July 13,
2022, to enable timely arrangements to be made.

II.

Facts

[
4
]

The facts in this section are not in dispute except
as noted.

A.

Background

[
5
]

The claimant has Bachelor’s and Master’s degree
in Fine Art.  At present, she works for the Vancouver Israeli Folk Society
teaching folk dancing.

[
6
]

The respondent is a physician specializing in
internal medicine.

[
7
]

The parties met at university in Israel in 2005.
They moved to New York City to further the respondent’s career, and married
there on December 4, 2006.

[
8
]

There are two children of the marriage: O. (born
2009), and N. (born 2013) (the “Children”).

[
9
]

The parties separated on January 1, 2017. On
February 1, 2018, the parties entered a comprehensive separation agreement that
addressed, among other things, parenting arrangements (the “Agreement”).  The
parties were divorced by an order pronounced August 31, 2018.

[
10
]

The parties moved to BC from New York City in 2010. They had planned
to reside in Vancouver, but the respondent failed to gain a licensing qualification
required to work at an urban hospital. He was qualified to take a position at a
rural hospital, so they moved to Gibsons.

[
11
]

The parties separated while living in Gibsons. Following separation,
the claimant moved to Vancouver and the respondent stayed in Gibsons. That is
where they respectively resided at the time of trial, although the claimant was
looking for a place on the North Shore.

[
12
]

The Agreement provides for shared parenting with a minimum of 40% of
the Children’s time spent with each parent. In practice, the parties seek to establish
a parenting time schedule that is equal. To date, they have come reasonably
close.

[
13
]

The parties agreed the Children would continue to attend school in
Gibsons following the separation. As of the trial, the regular school-year
parenting time schedule had the Children with the claimant from Thursday
evening through Sunday, and with the respondent from Sunday evening to Thursday.
The schedule was made feasible by the claimant’s home-schooling the Children on
Fridays. In order to bring the overall annual allocation near equal, the claimant
had the Children on professional development days, Monday statutory holidays, and
for a majority of the time during school breaks.

[
14
]

The dispute centres on the following Agreement
term (the “School Provision”):

4.4       Unless otherwise agreed to between
[the parties];

(a)        [O.]
will attend high-school on the 'North Shore’ (i.e. North or West Vancouver)
commencing in September 2022, and at that time [N.] will also attend school on
the North Shore. The Parties will consult with each other and need to agree on
which school the Child(ren) are to attend;

(b)        It
is expected that [the claimant] will be residing on the North Shore by
September 2022 so that [the Children] will be residing with [the claimant]
during the school week, while still maintaining a shared parenting schedule;
and

(c)        If
the Parties cannot agree as to which school the Child(ren) will attend and/or
how the shared parenting schedule needs to be amended to account for either
Parents’ possible change in residence, they will use the 'dispute resolution’
provisions set out in Section 12, herein.

[
15
]

The claimant seeks to enforce the School Provision and the
respondent seeks to vary it.

[
16
]

The parties re-partnered following their separation. Both new
partners have children of their own.

[
17
]

In March 2018, the claimant began living with T. T. has a daughter:
M. (born 2013). M. lives with the claimant and T. on a part-time basis under T.’s
shared parenting arrangement with M.’s mother.

[
18
]

In March 2018, the respondent began living with K. K. has two sons: A.
(born August 2009) and B. (born July 2013). The father of A. and B. also lives
in Gibsons, and he and K. have a shared parenting arrangement. Under that
arrangement, A. and B. live part-time with the respondent and K.

[
19
]

As it stands, A. and B. are at the respondent’s house from Sunday
afternoon through to Tuesday at 6:45 PM and every other Thursday, Friday and
Saturday. Thus, at present, O., N., A. and B. are all together at the
respondent’s house from Sunday evening through Tuesday dinner and during the
day on every other Thursday.

[
20
]

As it stands, M. is at the claimant’s house every Wednesday and
Thursday and on every other weekend. Thus, at present, O., N. and M. are all
together at the claimant’s house every Thursday evening and every other
weekend.

[
21
]

O. and N. get along well with A., B. and M.

[
22
]

O. and N. have positive relationships with K. and T.

[
23
]

The respondent works Monday through Friday and his hours vary. He
also has 10 on-call days each month, and during those days can be called in for
emergency work at any time (24 hours a day).

[
24
]

The claimant works approximately four hours a week. Those hours are
flexible and generally spread over two evenings a week.

[
25
]

O. has Crohn’s Disease. He takes medication and has a restricted
diet. O.’s medication recently changed to include an injection every two weeks.
He suffers some anxiety about the injections.

[
26
]

O. is quiet and studious by nature. N. is a social child who makes
friends easily. O. and N. both excel in academics. O. has a keen interest in
film-making, stop-motion production and similar subjects.

[
27
]

A. is an outdoorsy and outgoing child. Notwithstanding their
contrasting personalities, O. and A. have developed a close friendship.

[
28
]

O. and A. were in the same class in middle school. They will both enter
high school in September 2022.  Class schedules are idiosyncratic at the high
school level in Gibsons.

B.

Bolgar Report

[
29
]

The parties entered a consent order dated November 18, 2021 (“Consent
Order”). The Consent Order required an “evaluative” Views of the Child Report regarding
the possible implementation of the School Provision. The terms of the Consent
Order specifically required the report to include an assessment of whether the
Children’s views had been influenced.

[
30
]

Dr. Ellie Bolgar filed a report under
s. 211
of the
FLA
on
February 28, 2022 (“Bolgar Report”). The trial reconvened to enable Dr. Bolgar
to be cross-examined and to hear argument on her report and testimony. (As the respondent
ultimately endorsed the Bolgar Report, his questions were in the nature of
direct examination.)

[
31
]

I do not intend to canvas the claimant’s objections to the Bolger
Report. I do note that the cross-examination sought was warranted and that the clarification
obtained by having Dr. Bolgar testify was of assistance to the Court.

[
32
]

The essentials of Dr. Bolgar’s evidence are as follows: The Children
love and respect both parties and are happy at both of their homes. The
Children expressed concern about attending schools where they did not know
anyone, about not knowing where they would be living on the North Shore, and
about negotiating the route between home and school. O. expressed particular
concern about losing his connection with A. Both Children said they would prefer
to attend school in Gibsons, but indicated a willingness to accept whatever
decision was made.

III.

Positions

A.

The Claimant

[
33
]

The claimant submits that the Children are both very bright and
academically inclined and will significantly benefit from attending any of the strong
academic schools in West Vancouver and North Vancouver proposed. She says that
O., in particular, will benefit from attending a school offering advanced
preparation and advanced placement courses for university. She proposes he
attend a high school offering significant Advanced Placement courses or an
International Baccalaureate program. She notes that the proposed schools offer
diverse extracurricular programs, including in the subject area of film
production.  The claimant also submits that her work schedule enables her to be
home with the Children after school hours.

[
34
]

The claimant also contends that residing on the North Shore during
the school week will enable the Children to more fully interact with the Vancouver
Jewish community and culture. Her evidence is that they would be able to take Jewish
education, participate in Jewish youth programs, and observe and participate in
more Jewish ceremonies and celebrations.

B.

The Respondent

[
35
]

The respondent submits that attending school on the North Shore will
be disruptive and destabilizing for the Children. He posits that it will be
difficult for them to adapt to new schools, to adapt to living on the North
Shore on school days and, for O. in particular, to make new friends. He
stresses that Gibsons is the option the Children themselves prefer.

[
36
]

The respondent maintains the Children have built strong
relationships with K., A. and B., and that it is against their best interests
to alter those relationships. With regard to O. and A. in particular, the
respondent portrays the boys as closely bonded. He attests that they play
together constantly and that this has been helpful to O., describing him as
having become more outgoing and confident under A.’s influence.

[
37
]

The respondent contends that the proposed North Shore schools are
not significantly better than the schools in Gibsons. He notes that the Gibsons
high school does offer one advanced placement class (calculus), that children
go on to university from the Gibsons high school, and that there are some film-related
activities in Gibsons.

[
38
]

The respondent testified that there are now several Jewish families
in Gibsons, and they often join together to celebrate Jewish holidays. He
maintains that the Children can observe the holidays and participate in Jewish
culture during their time in Gibsons.

[
39
]

He notes that the Children’s physician and dentist are located in
Gibsons.

[
40
]

Finally, the respondent argues that the uncertainty as to where the
claimant will reside on the North Shore and what the schools the Children would
attend render it impossible to conclude that enforcing the School Provision would
be in the Children’s best interests.

IV.

Legal Framework

[
41
]

Section 44
of the
FLA
includes the following:

Agreements respecting parenting
arrangements

44   (1)Two or more of a child's guardians
may make an agreement respecting one or more of the following:

(a) the allocation
of parental responsibilities;

(b) parenting
time;

(c) the implementation
of an agreement made under this section;

(d) the means for
resolving disputes respecting an agreement made under this section.

...

(4) On application by a party, the court
must set aside or replace with an order made under this Division all or part of
an agreement respecting parenting arrangements
if satisfied that the
agreement is not in the best interests of the child
.

[Emphasis added.]

[
42
]

Section 37
of the
FLA
addresses the assessment of best
interests.  It provides:

Best interests of child

37

(1)
In making an agreement or order under this Part respecting
guardianship, parenting arrangements or contact with a child, the parties and the
court must consider the best interests of the child only.

(2)
To determine
what is in the best interests of a child,
all of
the child's needs and circumstances
must be
considered, including the following:

(a)
the child's health and emotional well-being;

(b)
the child's views, unless it would be inappropriate to
consider them;

(c)
the nature and strength of the relationships between
the child and significant persons in the child's life;

(d)
the history of the child's care;

(e)
the child's need for stability, given the child's age
and stage of development;

(f)
the ability of each person who is a guardian or seeks
guardianship of the child, or who has or seeks parental responsibilities,
parenting time or contact with the child, to exercise his or her
responsibilities;

(g)
the impact of any family violence on the child's
safety, security or well-being, whether the family violence is directed toward
the child or another family member;

(h)
whether the actions of a person responsible for family
violence indicate that the person may be impaired in his or her ability to care
for the child and meet the child's needs;

(i)
the appropriateness of an arrangement that would
require the child's guardians to cooperate on issues affecting the child,
including whether requiring cooperation would increase any risks to the safety,
security or well-being of the child or other family members;

(j)
any civil or criminal proceeding relevant to the
child's safety, security or well-being.

(3)
An agreement
or order is not in the best interests of a child unless it protects, to the
greatest extent possible, the child's physical, psychological and emotional
safety, security and well-being.

(4)
In making an
order under this Part, a court may consider a person's conduct only if it
substantially affects a factor set out in subsection (2), and only to the
extent that it affects that factor.

[
43
]

The parties differ at to whether the Agreement
itself can be considered as a factor in the
s. 44(4)
analysis.

[
44
]

The claimant, relying on
Dosch v. Wimmer
,

2021 BCSC 2167
at para.
22
(citing
Leiding v. Leiding
,
2016 BCSC 2567
), argues
that deference can be extended to the Agreement in the analysis:

[22]
In
Leiding
,
at para.
29
, Justice Harris
noted
a degree of deference
for the
agreement parties negotiate and enter:

[29]        While
I accept that the
Family Law Act
does not expressly incorporate the
“material change in circumstance test” for variations of an agreement regarding
parenting arrangements, in my view, it does not follow that the courts have an
unbridled authority to vary such agreements at the request of one party. In
Miglin
v. Miglin
,
2003 SCC 24 (CanLII)
, [2003] 1 S.C.R. 303, and subsequent jurisprudence, the courts
have emphasized that separation agreements, even in the unique circumstances of
separation and divorce, are nonetheless contracts and should be given effect
to: the courts should set aside the wishes of the parties as expressed in an
agreement only where it is shown that the agreement
fails to be in
substantial compliance
with the applicable legislative scheme. Although
Miglin

was decided in the context of spousal support, the principles expressed therein
indicate that there
must be compelling circumstances
for overriding what
the parties agreed to.

[Emphases added.]

[
45
]

The respondent disagrees.

[
46
]

In a case cited by neither party,
B.A.C. v. K.C
.,
2018 BCSC
2111
, Gomery J. expressly considered
Leiding
, paras.
29-32
(see
B.A.C
.
at para.
65
). In
B.A.C
., those paragraphs were argued to support the
proposition that “the court should be reluctant to change a parenting
arrangement contained in an agreement absent a material change of circumstances.”
Gomery J. concluded that those paragraphs of
Leiding
were
obiter
dictum
. He went on to reject the argument that the court should be reluctant
to change an agreement, instead adopting the reasons given in
Niijar v. Gill
,

2017 BCSC 1362
at paras.
102-113
, and
S.C.B. v. K.M.B
.,
2018 BCSC 1148

at paras.
51-53
.

[
47
]

I agree that
Leiding
para.
29
is
obiter
dictum
. With
respect to
Dosch
’s citation of it, neither
Leiding
nor the concept
of deference were referred to in determining the variance application in
Dosch

(see paras.
24-25
). Thus, even assuming that the citation in
Dosch

amounted to an implicit approval of
Leiding
, para.
29
, that approval
would itself constitute
obiter dictum
.

[
48
]

In my view,
s. 37
does not allow the Court to
extend any deference of any kind to the Agreement as part of the s. 44
analysis.

[
49
]

In
Niijar
, Griffin J. (as she then was),
stated as follows:

[111]     ... The
Respondent does not need to show a material change in circumstances. I accept
that the Respondent has framed the legal test correctly in respect of the
issues surrounding guardianship and parenting, namely: what are the best
interests of the Child.

[112]     The fact
that the Parenting Agreement was entered into and the parties operated under it
for several years is
one of the background facts
I can take into account
when considering the best interests of the Child. But no court has yet passed
on the issue of the best interests of the Child and that is the paramount
consideration for this Court.

[Emphasis added.]

[
50
]

Griffin J.’s reasons in support of that conclusion included a consideration
of
FLA
, ss. 37(1) and
(3)
(see
Niijar
at para.
113
(f)).
Section
37(1)
makes the best interests of the child the
only
consideration on an
application under Part 4 of the
FLA
(which includes
s. 44
).
Section
37(3)
expressly reinforces that focus.

[
51
]

Giving weight to the parties’ contractual expectations, in the guise
of extending “deference” to the agreement in the
s. 44(4)
analysis, would be inconsistent
with
s. 37(1)
’s use of the word “only”. To paraphrase Griffin J., the existence
of an agreement is a background
fact
, not a
factor
.

[
52
]

The existing agreement is relevant to the s. 44(4) analysis to the
extent it may assist the court with the identification and assessment of needs
and circumstances in considering best interests.

[
53
]

Should the court, following a fresh and full consideration of best
interests, conclude that the available options present a “dead heat” in terms
of best interests, the tie will go to the agreement. That is not due to any
deference within the
s. 44(4)
best interests analysis. It is simply the
consequence of failing to discharge the
s. 44(4)
onus to satisfy the court that
the agreement is
not
in the best interests of the child.

V.

Decision

[
54
]

I will begin by clearing some matters out of the way.

[
55
]

First, both parties addressed
N.R.G. v. G.R.G
.,
2017 BCCA 407

at paras.
39-41
, in their submissions. The circumstances here are not akin to
those in
N.R.G
., where the trial court was found to have exercised
parental responsibilities by making specific decisions at first instance. Here,
the parties negotiated the School Provision. The matter before me is a
particular dispute under
s. 44(4)
regarding the enforcement of that term.

[
56
]

Second, the status quo is not an option. The agreement to split
parenting time during the school week depended on the claimant’s ability to
home-school. That arrangement cannot continue when O. is in high school. As of
September 2022, the Children need to attend school five days a week, and thus
must be in one place during school hours on school days. The issue is which of
the two possible versions of enabling that is in the Children’s best interests.

[
57
]

Finally, there are no family violence issues, the parties are
capable parents, and they are both capable of the cooperation needed to
co-parent. The best interests analysis here will focus on the
FLA
, s.
37(2)(a)-(c) and (e) considerations.

A.

The Bolgar Report

[
58
]

I find the Bolgar Report of assistance, albeit in a rather indirect manner.

[
59
]

Surprisingly, the Children were only told that they might go to
school on the North Shore shortly before their interviews. Further, given the
respondent’s position on the implementation of the School Provision, the called
for consultation did not take place, no North Shore schools were settled upon
and the claimant did not know where on North Shore she should live.

[
60
]

In the result, the Children were asked to express a preference
between a vague hypothetical and something familiar. Dr. Bolgar agreed those
circumstances would likely have a significant impact on their expressed
preferences.

[
61
]

What is informative, however, is that even in those circumstances
the Children’s preferences were tempered and both indicated a willingness to comply
with the decision ultimately made. All things considered, I find the Children’s
views on the matter to be fairly neutral.

[
62
]

I would not be inclined to place much weight on the preferences expressed
in any event. The Bolgar Report failed to address whether the Children had been
influenced. Dr. Bolgar testified that she would have commented had she concluded
the Children were influenced. That does not satisfy me she turned her mind to
the issue and explored it adequately with the Children. I note that I share the
claimant’s skepticism given the respondent’s knowing disregard of my witness
exclusion order.

B.

The Resiliency of the Children

[
63
]

Much of the respondent’s argument rests on his assertion that the
Children will find it difficult to deal with change. The evidence does not bear
out that assertion.

[
64
]

The Children adapted to the separation, to the claimant’s move to
Vancouver, and to moving out of the previous family home in Gibsons. O. saw a
counsellor very briefly following the separation, but had no need to continue.
N. did not have any counselling. The Children readily accepted their parents’
new partners, as well as those partners’ children. They have successfully
merged into two new blended families and now happily reside in two households where
step-siblings come and go over the course of each week. Throughout these many
changes, the Children have thrived.

[
65
]

O. has a circle of friends in Gibsons. While he has not made friends
in Vancouver to date, he has neither attended school in Vancouver nor been
involved in regular programs and activities there, which are common
opportunities to make friends. While O. is a naturally quiet child, he has become
more confident and more social in recent years. N. is a quite social child who
interacts with ease, and neither party has concern about her ability to make
new friends at a new school.

[
66
]

In my view, the Children are very resilient and deal well with
change.

C.

Maintaining Relationships

[
67
]

The respondent contends that a move from the present parenting
schedule to a North Shore school parenting schedule will fundamentally alter
his relationship with the Children. I do not accept that. The Agreement
provides for a 40% minimum allocation. The practice of trying to set an annual
50/50 overall allocation will continue. The respondent failed to explain how or
why it is that he would be unable to maintain his connection to the Children
and his involvement in their lives if they do not spend mid-week evenings with
him during the school year.  Since separation, both parties have fully
maintained their relationships with the Children.

[
68
]

No matter where the Children attend school, the change to the
parenting-time schedule required for full-time attendance will impact the
present pattern of overlap with A., B. and M.  No matter where the Children
attend school, the changed schedule will continue to result in significant
overlapping household time with A., B. and M. (There is also the reality that A.,
B. and M.’s shared parenting arrangements may themselves vary over time.)

[
69
]

The respondent overstates the impact that a North Shore school
schedule would have on the Children’s relationships with A., B. and K. The
Children and A. and B. have only ever had partially overlapping days in the respondent’s
house. They will continue to have overlap, albeit on different days. K. will
continue to be in the household whenever the Children are in Gibsons.

[
70
]

Even if O. went to high school in Gibsons, he and A. would not be in
the same classes. A North Shore school schedule would give O. and A. the
ability to socialize on weekends, which is in keeping with peer socialization
at the high school level. Further, given that A.’s father lives in Gibsons, O.
and A. will likely be able to spend time together even on weekends when A. is
at his father’s house. There is a good chance that a North Shore school
schedule would allow O. and A. to actually spend more time together than a
Gibsons school schedule would.

[
71
]

Finally, K. is a teacher at a middle school in Gibsons. She does not
work on weekends or school breaks.  Under a North Shore school schedule, the
Children’s time on Gibsons would be weighted toward weekends, school holidays
and school breaks, all periods when K., A. and B. would have time to socialize.

D.

Jewish Community and Cultural Involvement

[
72
]

I accept the respondent’s evidence that some Jewish families in
Gibsons now observe Jewish holidays together. That experience is different,
however, from the more involved type of Jewish education and youth programs
experience addressed in the claimant’s evidence.

[
73
]

I am satisfied that it would be beneficial for the Children to have
the experience of participating in the more in-depth cultural and community
activities described by the claimant. Those activities will enable them to more
fully experience the Jewish culture and to better relate to their extended
family, many of whom continue to live in Israel. I note that the Agreement
specifically provides for the Children to visit Israel and their family there.

E.

Attending a School with Advanced Academics

[
74
]

The claimant and respondent are university educated. The Children
are being raised in families that value post-secondary education. Both parties have
academic and educational expectations for the Children. I am satisfied that these
shared expectations informed the agreement to include the School Provision in
the Agreement.

[
75
]

Without doubt, many children from the Gibsons high school will go on
to post-secondary education. The issue is not the comparative quality of the
school programs in the abstract. The question here is particular: what is in O.
and N.’s best interests?

[
76
]

O. is a very bright child, is studious by nature and enjoys academic
pursuits. He also has a keen area of interest – film-making – that lends itself
to group work, including through clubs and programs. Those facts persuade me
that O., as a high school student, would be better-served attending a school with
a focus on academic achievement, that offers advanced courses and programs, and
has specialized extra-curricular activities.

[
77
]

While N.’s interests and strengths are less clear at this time, she
is also a bright child and will likely benefit from an academic focus in turn.
She will, in any event, benefit from having a parenting-time schedule that
matches O.’s.

[
78
]

Although specific schools have yet to be identified, that is because
the respondent’s position displaced the School Provision consultation. The
claimant has identified the type of schools under contemplation and the type of
programs they offer. She will choose a North Shore neighbourhood depending on
the selected schools. That is sufficient to enable the best interests
assessment to be made in the circumstances of this case.

F.

Health-related Matters

[
79
]

O. has a serious health issue. Both parties are very attentive to
it. The respondent, as a physician, is well-positioned to monitor O.’s condition
and continuity of care. His anxiety about injections is being addressed and is
not a factor here.

[
80
]

If it is necessary for the Children to continue to see their present
physician or dentist in Gibsons, the claimant’s employment enables her to take
the Children to Gibsons during the school week. If that continuity is
unnecessary, and it is more convenient for the Children see more conveniently
located health-care providers during the school week, replacement providers can
be agreed upon through consultation.

VI.

DISPOSITION

[
81
]

On consideration of all of the above, I am satisfied that it is in the
Children’s best interests for the School Provision of the Agreement to be
enforced.
